answer.evidence: Most first-layer units (0, 3-7, 9, 13-15, 19, 22, 24, 25, 28, 30, 31) look like barely-trained random filters: integer weights spread roughly uniformly in ±80 with no spatial structure. The units with clearly trained structure (weights reaching ±85-99) encode centre-versus-surround patterns, not compact patches. Unit 20 has a strong positive blob over rows 10-17, cols 6-12 (99, 92, 96, 91) and negatives near the top and bottom borders (r2-3, r22-23). Unit 18 is positive over central rows 9-17. Unit 8 is positive over the central and lower-central rows. Unit 16 has its strongest negative weights (-84 to -92) concentrated in rows 8-20, plus a few at the edges. Unit 17 is the reverse of unit 20: negative centre (r8-12 down to -95) and positive top and bottom rows. Unit 23 is positive along the top rows, left column and bottom row. Unit 1 is uniformly about +30 across the whole image. Approximate output effects through W2·W3, ignoring ReLU gating: unit 18 about +30k, unit 1 +17k, units 8, 20 and 27 about +7k to +9k (all toward malignant); unit 16 about -20k and the high-bias unit 26 about -15k (toward benign); units 17 and 23 roughly neutral. I scanned all four corners and the borders for a compact same-sign block of large weights shared across units, as a fixed marker or text artifact would produce; none exists, and the large weights are scattered rather than clustered. The ±80 random-init range limits sensitivity, so a weak shortcut cannot be fully ruled out.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly responds to bright, dense tissue in the centre of the crop: a large, solid nodule pushes toward malignant (units 18, 20, 8) and overall image brightness adds to this (unit 1). A dark, air-filled centre and the high-bias unit 26 push toward benign.
